data.content_ref: inline:{"analogy":{"adopted_commitment_refs":[],"disanalogies":["In medical triage, survival is the direct goal, whereas in Popperian science, truth approximation is the goal and survival of the theory is secondary to falsification","Chess openings rely on statistical databases of opponent errors (inductive), whereas Popper explicitly rejects using past frequency to predict future moves"],"overturn_conditions":["If it can be shown that medical triage implicitly relies on Bayesian probability updates rather than simple track-record heuristics","If chess masters are proven to act solely on intuition devoid of pattern recognition from past games"],"shared_structure":["Decision made under uncertainty without probabilistic guarantees","Preference based on past performance/resistance to failure rather than predicted future success","Goal is to maximize learning/error detection rather than ensure immediate safety"],"source_memory_refs":["medical_triage_protocol","chess_opening_preparation"],"transfer_claims":["Just as a doctor chooses the treatment with the best track record not because it guarantees cure but because it is the most robust known option, a scientist chooses the best-corroborated theory as the most robust basis for action","Both domains accept that the chosen path may fail catastrophically, but deviating from the best-tested path would be irrational negligence"]},"claim":"Popper's preference for better-corroborated theories in practical action is defensible without smuggling in induction, provided one accepts a 'critical rationalist' normative bridge: acting on the best-tested theory is not a prediction of success (which would require induction) but the only rational way to expose error if the theory is false. The cost of this defense is the abandonment of 'practical security'; the agent must admit that the bridge built on the best-tested theory might still collapse tomorrow, and that choosing it offers no probabilistic guarantee of safety, only the satisfaction of having subjected the decision to the severest possible critique.","counterconditions":[{"case":"If the agent requires a guarantee of practical success (e.g., the bridge must not fall) rather than just a guarantee of rational procedure, the Popperian defense fails.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"},{"case":"If 'acting on' a theory logically entails believing it is probably true, then Popper's distinction collapses and induction is smuggled back in.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"},{"case":"If the cost of error is infinite (e.g., human extinction), the lack of probabilistic assurance in Popper's framework may render the preference irrational despite its methodological purity.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"}],"definitions":[],"derivation":[],"formalization_refs":[],"mechanism":"The mechanism distinguishes between 'justification of belief' (which Popper rejects as requiring induction) and 'justification of action' (which relies on methodological rules). By framing action as an extension of the testing process\u2014where choosing Theory A over Theory B is a bet that allows us to learn faster if A is wrong\u2014the preference becomes a procedural imperative rather than an inductive inference. This resolves the tension by redefining 'preference' from 'expectation of truth' to 'commitment to the most rigorous available standard of criticism.'","premises":[],"schema":"deepreason-reasoning-envelope-v1","scope":{"covers":[],"excludes":[]},"simulation_refs":[],"uncertainties":[]}
